notes: Landmark fixed/floating charge appeal; Siebe Gorman analysis and Agnew/New Bullas precedent discussion are explicit throughout.

enrichment.short_title: Fixed charge over book debts in Siebe Gorman debenture upheld

statutes_considered.title: Preferential Payments in Bankruptcy Amendment Act 1897

key_facts: Spectrum Plus Ltd granted NatWest a standard debenture over its book debts to secure a fluctuating overdraft facility for working capital.
The company went into creditors' voluntary liquidation and the liquidators refused to account for collected book debts to the bank.
The Vice-Chancellor held the debenture created a floating rather than a fixed charge, prioritising preferential creditors over the bank.
The appeal turned on whether Slade J was correct in Siebe Gorman that similar debenture wording created a fixed charge despite the chargor collecting and using proceeds.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from a Vice-Chancellor's declaration application under section 112 Insolvency Act 1986 on the nature of a bank debenture charge.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; the debenture created a fixed charge over book debts and Siebe Gorman was correctly decided, notwithstanding conflict with Agnew and constraints of Re New Bullas precedent.
enrichment.ratio: Where a debenture prohibits disposal of book debts before collection and requires proceeds to be paid into an account with the chargee bank, the charge may properly be categorised as fixed even if the chargor may draw on the account within agreed limits; payment of book debts into an overdrawn loan account means the company never controlled the proceeds as free cash flow.
legal_issues: Whether a charge over book debts permitting collection and use of proceeds is fixed or floating
Whether Re New Bullas or Agnew should be followed on precedent
Whether Siebe Gorman was correctly decided
Effect of Insolvency Act preferential creditor priority on charge categorisation
linked_authorities: Siebe Gorman & Co Ltd v Barclays Bank Ltd [1979] 2 Lloyd's Rep 142
Agnew v Commissioner of Inland Revenue [2001] UKPC 28
Re New Bullas Trading Ltd [1994] 1 BCLC 485

confidence.notes: Outcome, statutory framework, and charge categorisation reasoning are fully articulated. House of Lords permission was not sought.

notes: Conjoined CICAP judicial reviews on real consent and crime of violence; CD dismissed and JM succeeded on distinct fact patterns.

enrichment.short_title: Criminal injuries compensation and real consent in sexual offence claims
key_facts: Two conjoined judicial review applications challenged Criminal Injuries Compensation Appeals Panel refusals to award compensation.
CD, aged almost 13, claimed unlawful sexual intercourse by a 21-year-old man who pleaded guilty; the panel found she had given real consent.
JM claimed repeated indecent assault by her foster mother's son over 12–18 months from about age 12; the panel found a consensual boyfriend-girlfriend relationship.
Both cases turned on whether the applicants were non-consenting victims of a crime of violence under the 1996 Compensation Scheme.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Conjoined judicial review of two Criminal Injuries Compensation Appeals Panel decisions refusing compensation.
enrichment.outcome: CD's application dismissed; JM's application succeeded and the panel decision was quashed for failure properly to assess vulnerability and real consent.
enrichment.ratio: A crime of violence requires absence of real consent freely and voluntarily given; where vulnerability is asserted the panel must assess imbalance in the relationship, relative responsibility, and whether conduct amounted to submission rather than consent, and cannot justify refusal solely by incomplete medical disclosure when the school or panel knew of the disability.
legal_issues: Meaning of crime of violence under the Criminal Injuries Compensation Scheme
Whether real consent excludes eligibility for compensation
Proper approach to panel reasoning and post-decision witness statements
Whether subsequent statutory changes may be taken into account
linked_authorities: R (August) v Criminal Injuries Compensation Appeal Panel [2001] QB 774
R (on the application of JE) v Criminal Injuries Compensation Appeals Panel [2003] EWCA Civ 237
R v Criminal Injuries Compensation Board, ex parte Webb [1987] 1 QB 74

confidence.notes: Scheme provisions, August/JE principles, and split outcomes are clear. Some panel fact findings involve sensitive credibility assessments.

notes: Case stated on magistrates' jurisdiction under section 33 Child Support Act; statutory scheme and Shotton followed.

enrichment.short_title: Magistrates cannot review child support liability on liability order application
key_facts: Mr Farley separated from his wife in 1990 under a deed providing £15 per week maintenance per child.
The Child Support Agency assessed substantial arrears of £32,639.94 and applied for a liability order under section 33.
Farley argued he was not liable because of the pre-1993 maintenance agreement or because section 6 benefits conditions were unmet.
The magistrates' court held it could not determine initial liability and made the liability order.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal by case stated from a magistrates' court liability order under section 33 Child Support Act 1991, with an extension of time granted for filing.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; the magistrates' court's sole function was to decide whether assessed payments had become payable and were unpaid, not whether child support maintenance was payable in the first place.
enrichment.ratio: Section 33(4) precludes the magistrates' court from questioning the validity of a maintenance assessment; questions of liability and quantification must be pursued through the Act's review and appeal structure, and the court's only task is to confirm arrears accumulation.
legal_issues: Scope of magistrates' court jurisdiction under section 33 Child Support Act 1991
Whether liability to pay child support may be challenged on a liability order application
Effect of a pre-1993 written maintenance agreement under section 4(10)
Whether section 6 benefit conditions must be proved before enforcement
index_terms: Secretary of State for Social Security v Shotton
linked_authorities: Secretary of State for Social Security v Shotton [1996] 2 FLR 241

confidence.notes: Statutory interpretation and outcome are straightforward. Limited discussion of section 20 appeal routes.

notes: Second habeas corpus extradition challenge; partial discharge on misdescribed terrorist charges but s.11(3) bar on full discharge.

enrichment.short_title: Spanish extradition: partial discharge for misdescribed bomb charges
key_facts: Castillo, a Spanish citizen, was arrested at Dover and sought for extradition on alleged Basque terrorist offences including placing an explosive under a police officer's car.
Spain withdrew one barracks explosion charge after evidence showed a map was of the applicant's home, not the target.
The extradition request inaccurately described conduct suggesting attempted murder of an officer who was in his house, not near the car.
Full Spanish court dossier materials later showed the device was manually lit, found 150m away, and unlikely to endanger life as pleaded.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Second habeas corpus application challenging lawfulness of committal for extradition to Spain under the European Convention on Extradition.
enrichment.outcome: Applicant discharged on extradition charges 6 and 7 (attempted murder and GBH to police officer) but application failed on charges 1–3 and 5; section 11(3) did not require full discharge.
enrichment.ratio: A requesting state must fairly and accurately describe conduct under Article 12 of the European Convention on Extradition; where dossier materials show a misdescription, equivalent UK offences of attempted murder or GBH may not be made out, but bad faith requires more than careless drafting, and discharge under section 11(3) requires success in relation to every offence.
legal_issues: Whether extradition conduct descriptions under Article 12 were accurate and fair
Whether accusations were made in good faith under section 11(3)(c)
Whether described conduct constituted equivalent UK attempt offences
Whether partial discharge is available when only some charges fail
linked_authorities: R (Saifi) v Governor of Brixton Prison [2001] 1 WLR 1134

confidence.notes: Partial outcome and Article 12 reasoning are clear. Complex multi-charge extradition facts required selective summarisation.

notes: Procedural ruling on Chadwick LJ costs order restricting enforcement; permission for sale application not required.

enrichment.short_title: No permission needed to enforce charging order by sale after s.459 costs
key_facts: Arrow Nominees and Mrs Tobias lost a section 459 unfair prejudice petition against the Blackledge majority shareholders in Bodycare Ltd.
The Court of Appeal ordered interim costs of £750,000 payable only by charging order over 240 shares each, with enforcement otherwise requiring Chadwick LJ's permission.
Mrs Tobias's shares were sold cheaply by her trustee in bankruptcy; the Blackledge parties sought to enforce a charging order over Arrow Nominees' shares by sale.
Mr Tobias applied to vary a direction granting permission to apply for sale, concerned about undervaluation.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application to vary or confirm directions on whether prior Court of Appeal permission was required before applying for sale under a charging order enforcing an interim costs order.
enrichment.outcome: Permission to apply for an order for sale was not required under the July 2000 costs order; the Manchester County Court may determine sale terms including price and conduct.
enrichment.ratio: A direction restricting enforcement of an interim costs order to charging orders over specified shares did not require further permission from the Court of Appeal before applying under CPR Part 73 for sale of charged property; the restriction was aimed at preventing bankruptcy or other enforcement without court oversight.
legal_issues: Construction of interim costs order restricting enforcement to charging orders
Whether charging order sale requires prior permission of the costs judge
Jurisdiction of county court on application for order for sale under CPR 73

confidence.notes: Procedural holding is explicit. Underlying unfair prejudice merits are not re-decided.

notes: Administration directions on pension scheme withdrawal; section 75 MFR vs buy-out liability analysis detailed.

enrichment.short_title: Administrators permitted to withdraw subsidiaries from asbestos pension scheme
key_facts: T&N Limited and eleven subsidiaries were in administration within the Federal-Mogul group following asbestos-related insolvency.
The T&N Retirement Benefits Scheme had about 37,633 members and a potential buy-out deficit of some £875 million.
Administrators sought to withdraw associated companies before trustees wound up the scheme or adopted a gilts-matching policy, limiting section 75 liability to the MFR basis.
Withdrawal could increase distributions to associated company creditors from as low as 11.6% to up to 100% on some scenarios.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Administration application for directions on whether administrators may cause associated companies to withdraw from a multi-employer pension scheme.
enrichment.outcome: Administrators directed that they may give withdrawal notice; withdrawal is in creditors' interests and does not breach Ex parte James dishonourable conduct principles or anticipated Pensions Bill contribution notices.
enrichment.ratio: Where associated companies lawfully may withdraw from a multi-employer scheme and thereby avoid a future buy-out section 75 liability that does not yet exist, administrators owe no duty to trustees to refrain from withdrawal; acting to protect creditors by preventing crystallisation of a larger liability is not dishonourable under Ex parte James.
legal_issues: Administrators' duty to creditors versus pension scheme trustees' interests
Section 75 deficiency liability on MFR basis versus buy-out basis
Effect of scheme winding up or gilts-matching investment policy
Application of Ex parte James dishonourable conduct principle
Relevance of draft Pensions Bill contribution notices
linked_authorities: Ex parte James [1874] LR 9 Ch App 609

confidence.notes: Funding calculations and legal conclusions are well evidenced. Draft Pensions Bill treatment is explicitly provisional.

notes: Leading Part 36 payment withdrawal authority; Manku v Seehra approach adopted over automatic stay.

enrichment.short_title: Part 36 payment acceptance valid despite defendant's reduction application
key_facts: A firefighter injured in a road traffic accident issued a personal injury claim; the defendant admitted liability.
The defendant paid £24,500 into court under Part 36 before receiving a further medical report suggesting lower damages.
The defendant applied to reduce the payment and notified withdrawal; the claimant accepted the original payment within 21 days.
The judge held acceptance was unjust because the defendant's application automatically suspended the acceptance period.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Second appeal from county court on construction of Part 36 CPR and discretion to permit withdrawal or reduction of a Part 36 payment.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; no automatic stay arises from a defendant's application to reduce a Part 36 payment, but permission to reduce should be refused where the only change is a further expert report and the claimant validly accepted within 21 days.
enrichment.ratio: Rule 36.6(5) requires court permission to withdraw or reduce a Part 36 payment and applies to the offer comprised in the payment; a claimant may accept within 21 days even if the defendant has applied to reduce, and the court should follow Manku v Seehra by deciding the application in light of acceptance rather than implying an automatic suspension.
legal_issues: Whether a defendant's application to reduce a Part 36 payment suspends the 21-day acceptance period
Construction of rules 36.6(5) and 36.11 CPR
Discretionary test for permission to withdraw or reduce a Part 36 payment
Whether Part 36 payments are contractual offers

confidence.notes: Ratio on Part 36 construction and discretionary outcome are clearly stated. Medical evidence merits were not fully reviewed.

notes: Commercial Court wasted costs order against Clyde & Co for misleading letter on interim costs; £5,000 assessed.

enrichment.short_title: Wasted costs order against solicitors for misleading interim costs letter
key_facts: Crown Resources lost an arbitration and Cooke J dismissed its permission to appeal with costs in March 2004.
Holman Fenwick & Willan obtained a paper interim costs order of about £6,000 after no response from Clyde & Co.
Clyde & Co wrote asserting their client wished to make representations, causing the court to revoke the order; the client had been declared bankrupt in Switzerland on 11 June.
Morison J found Clyde & Co had no express instructions for the letter and had misled the court.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application for wasted costs order against former solicitors under CPR against the background of enforcement of arbitration costs.
enrichment.outcome: Wasted costs order made for £5,000 against Clyde & Co; the letter of 17 June 2004 unreasonably asserted instructions to oppose interim costs when none existed.
enrichment.ratio: Solicitors act unreasonably and may be liable in wasted costs where they tell the court their client wishes to make representations on an interim costs order without express instructions, thereby causing unnecessary costs, even if arising from over-enthusiasm rather than deliberate misconduct.
legal_issues: Threshold for wasted costs orders against solicitors
Whether solicitors had authority to write opposing interim costs enforcement
Effect of client's Swiss bankruptcy on retainer
Proportionality of wasted costs award

confidence.notes: Findings on instructions and costs assessment are explicit. Underlying arbitration merits are not discussed.

notes: Large fraud amendment application with partial permission; some Hollywood 1/2 pleading formulations refused pending re-draft.

enrichment.short_title: Partial permission to plead broker fraud in Hollywood film insurance claims
key_facts: HIH sought to amend consolidated claims against broker JLT to allege fraudulent misrepresentation and non-disclosure in placing pecuniary loss indemnity policies for Hollywood film slates 1–3.
Claims against reinsurers had failed on warranty issues; JLT became sole defendant with sums of about US$15.6m, US$14.7m and US$25.1m at stake.
HIH relied on TNP and later Hollywood placements as similar-fact evidence and on materials from settled Hollywood 4/5 litigation.
JLT opposed late fraud amendments on delay, prejudice, and pleading inadequacy grounds.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application for permission to amend pleadings to add fraud claims in consolidated Commercial Court proceedings against an insurance broker.
enrichment.outcome: Permission granted in principle to plead fraud subject to costs sanctions; specific Hollywood 1 and 2 due diligence, reliability, and escrow account formulations refused pending re-draft; TNP similar-fact evidence admitted for Hollywood 3.
enrichment.ratio: There is no special rule against late amendments to plead fraud; permission should be granted unless prejudice cannot be compensated by costs, but fraud pleading must be sufficiently particularised and similar-fact evidence requires probative value and a sufficient primary case on the impugned transaction.
legal_issues: Whether late fraud amendments should be permitted
Admissibility of TNP allegations as similar-fact evidence
Particularisation requirements for deceit pleading
Whether agents must disclose their own fraud under section 19 Marine Insurance Act 1906

PCW Syndicates v PCW Reinsurers [1996] 1 Lloyd's Rep 241

notes: SEND tribunal disability discrimination appeal; Collins J quashed reasoning on work placement medical form.

enrichment.short_title: School unlawfully discriminated on visually impaired pupil's work placement

statutes_considered.title: Special Educational Needs and Disability Act 2001

key_facts: D, a visually impaired year 10 pupil at Plymouth High School for Girls, needed to see at 6 metres what others see at 18 metres and had a statement of special educational needs.
All year 10 pupils were encouraged to choose work placements; D selected media, her former primary school, and animal care options.
The medical condition question on the placement form was left blank because D disliked attention to her disability; the school knew of her impairment but failed to pass information to Trident.
All three choices were rejected at a matching meeting without adequate consultation; Trident refused placement without medical disclosure.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from Special Educational Needs and Disability Tribunal decision rejecting disability discrimination complaint about work experience placement allocation.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; declaration that the school unlawfully discriminated against D; tribunal reasoning that non-disclosure justified treatment could not stand.
enrichment.ratio: Less favourable treatment relating to disability is not justified where the school knew of the pupil's visual impairment and failed reasonably to take section 28C steps before placements were allocated; blaming the pupil for an incomplete medical form when the school should have disclosed known information and consulted cannot justify discriminatory placement decisions.
legal_issues: Whether failure to allocate work placements amounted to disability discrimination under section 28A DDA 1995
Whether treatment was justified under section 28B
Reasonable adjustments duty under section 28C
Proper comparator between disabled and non-disabled pupils

confidence.notes: Statutory framework and Collins J's rejection of tribunal reasoning are clear. Remedy limited to declaration rather than remittal.
